panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Human brain MRI directly demonstrating the pathognomonic molar tooth sign of Joubert syndrome, explicitly identified by the caption and white arrow. B: Human retinal image showing retinal dystrophy with maculopathy, a captioned ocular manifestation of Joubert syndrome. C: Human fundus image directly showing an optic-disc coloboma, which corresponds to the disease-specific chorioretinal coloboma category and is explicitly associated with Joubert syndrome by the caption and review context.

panels.figure_caption: Representative clinical ocular presentations of Joubert Syndrome. (A) Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) T2-weighted image of the “Molar Tooth Sign” (white arrow). (B) Retinal dystrophy with maculopathy. (C) Coloboma of the optic disc, marked with a dashed line.
in_text_mentions: , and abnormal eye movements first described by Marie Joubert in 1969 [1,2,3]. It is accompanied by a congenital malformation of the brainstem and cerebellar vermis that composes the pathognomonic finding of a “molar tooth sign” (MTS) on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain (Figure 1A). Abnormal features that constitute MTS include cerebellar vermis hypoplasia, deepened interpeduncular fossa, and thickened and elongated superior cerebellar peduncles. There are many subtypes of JS and JS-related disorders where MTS is found that involve the brain, eyes, kidneys, liver, and limbs [4,5].

nt. Its pathogenesis places JS within an expanding spectrum of diseases termed ciliopathies [6,7]. Commonly found features in JS include ophthalmic and oculomotor abnormalities, which can be useful in establishing a diagnosis [2]. The diverse abnormal eye movements include strabismus, nystagmus, oculomotor apraxia, and vertical gaze palsy. Several case reports have described retinal abnormalities (Figure 1A–C); among them are retinitis pigmentosa (RP), retinal dystrophy, chorioretinal colobomas, and retinal blindness [8,9,10,11,12,13]. This review will detail the ophthalmologic findings of JS.
